#10735. Travel YouTuber dies after being struck by truck in hit-and-run during overseas trip

A South Korean travel YouTuber has died at the age of 33 after being struck by a truck while cycling through Bolivia, with the driver reportedly fleeing the scene.

According to Bolivian news outlet UNITEL, the accident occurred at approximately 9:30 AM on November 4 in the city of El Alto.

Witnesses rushed to help the YouTuber after he was struck by a large cargo truck, but his injuries were too severe, and he died at the scene.

The truck driver fled following the collision but was apprehended by police several hours later.

According to SBS News, the driver told investigators he had not seen the bicycle. Police also confirmed that a breathalyzer test detected no alcohol in his system.

Authorities are continuing to investigate the circumstances surrounding the fatal collision.

JinsTravel launched his YouTube channel in 2020, sharing videos of his cycling adventures across Europe, Africa, North America, and beyond.

He had recently been traveling through South America after beginning an ambitious journey from Mexico, with his final video uploaded on October 30 documenting his travels through Peru’s Andes Mountains.

On November 5, an acquaintance announced his death on his YouTube channel with permission from his family.

The acquaintance explained that Cho had spent years preparing for his dream journey, filming his travels and sharing them with viewers around the world.

Funeral arrangements are being prepared in Bolivia with assistance from the South Korean Embassy. The family has also requested that people refrain from sharing unverified speculation or footage of the accident.

Fans have since flooded his videos with condolences, with one viewer writing, “I hope you enjoy your travels in heaven.”

The tragedy comes just months after Thai travel YouTuber Hlun Solo was found dead in a hotel in Georgia, more than two weeks after his family lost contact with him.

#10733. New drinkable croissant turns breakfast pastry into a bottled latte

A Japanese beverage brand is releasing a new drink that pairs buttery pastry flavors of croissants with coffee, and it’s just as unique as it sounds.

Croissants and coffee are a staple pairing, especially for those who like a tasty breakfast or light lunch. However, have you ever wished you could capture the flavour profiles of both and enjoy them as a drink? No, me neither, but that hasn’t stopped Japanese drink maker Suntory from giving it a good old go.

Enter the Craft Boss Croissant Latte, a coffee-based drink that’s been designed to recreate the taste of enjoying a croissant and cafe latte all in one drink.

Developed in coordination with a Japanese bakery (Bread, Espresso &), the latte uses lightly roasted coffee beans with fruity notes alongside espresso ingredients. Milk and sugar provide the sweetness, while added salt helps recreate the rich taste of a croissant.

As for the pastry element, Suntory developed a flavoring designed to capture a croissant’s buttery aroma and toasted notes. Each 450ml bottle has a retail price of ¥270, which is around $1.70.

Those who prefer an actual croissant with their coffee can also try a matching menu item at participating Bread, Espresso & locations across Japan from November 10 to December 10. Priced at ¥900 (around $5.70), the cafe version features a croissant caramelized with honey butter and comes served with a foamy cafe latte blended with cream for dipping.

Interestingly, the drinkable croissant coffee isn’t the only eye-catching food item to come out of Japan this year. Back in May, Pizza Hut Japan revealed a “drinkable pizza” that combines melted cheese and rich curry sauce. This was then followed by a spicy noodle pizza that came topped with pork and cheese.

#10729. Spectrum offers free GTA 6 internet upgrade to download massive 212GB game in under 30 minutes

Spectrum is offering customers a free internet speed upgrade ahead of GTA 6’s launch, claiming it will allow players to download Rockstar’s massive 212GB game in less than 30 minutes.

With Grand Theft Auto 6 finally launching on November 19, fans are preparing for what could be one of the biggest gaming releases of all time. However, the game’s enormous file size has raised concerns about storage space and lengthy downloads.

Now, internet provider Spectrum is stepping in to make things a little easier, at least for eligible customers in the United States.

In a November 4 announcement, Spectrum revealed it is introducing a temporary “Gig Speed Lift” that will boost qualifying customers’ internet speeds at no additional cost.

“The most anticipated game in the world is almost ready to download, and Spectrum is treating eligible customers to a free Gig Speed Lift, November 9 to 30, that will have them cruising Vice City before the rest of the block finishes downloading. No cost, and no strings attached,” they said.

The promotion runs from November 9 through November 30, allowing customers with compatible equipment and eligible plans to activate the upgrade through the My Spectrum app.

Those who qualify will receive speeds of up to 1Gbps, while existing 1 Gig customers in select areas can receive an upgrade to 2Gbps.

Spectrum claims its 1 Gig service will allow players to download GTA 6 in under 30 minutes, although actual download times will depend on connection speeds, network conditions, and console download servers.

“With Spectrum Internet Gig, customers can start playing Grand Theft Auto VI in less than 30 minutes, so game day is for cruising, not downloading,” the company said.

GTA 6 file size revealed and players may want to start clearing storage space

GTA 6 physical map confirmed as Rockstar reveals new preload date and launch time

Rockstar admit they’re “nervous” about GTA 6 as they know it has to be “perfect”

The timing couldn’t be better, as Rockstar recently moved GTA 6’s preload date forward from November 12 to November 10, giving players nine days to download the game before launch.

The speed boost won’t grant early access, however, meaning everyone will still have to wait until their regional release time to actually play.

Spectrum says the promotion comes with no hidden fees or permanent changes to customers’ plans. Once November 30 arrives, internet speeds will automatically return to their original levels without customers needing to take action.

The offer is another sign of just how enormous GTA 6’s launch is expected to be, with recent estimates suggesting Rockstar has already generated more than $750 million in digital preorders.

GTA 6 launches November 19 for PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S.

#10725. Discord reveals major app overhaul that could make it faster and use less ram

Discord is working on a major overhaul of its desktop and mobile apps, with plans to rewrite its client using Rust in an effort to improve performance and reduce resource usage.

The company has already been using Rust for parts of its infrastructure and voice technology for years, but the latest effort aims to bring the programming language to the entire client.

The changes could affect how Discord runs across multiple platforms, including Windows, macOS, and mobile devices, while potentially addressing concerns about the app’s memory consumption.

On November 5, Discord co-founder and CTO Stanislav Vishnevskiy revealed that the company is working toward moving its entire client to Rust, a programming language known for its performance and memory safety.

“We’ve been early adopters of Rust since 2018 and a lot of our infra, voice tech, and even some of the current client is already Rust,” he wrote on X.

“The holy grail was getting the whole client there.”

According to Vishnevskiy, the transition would also involve moving away from Electron, the framework currently used for Discord’s desktop application, as well as React Native on mobile.

We've been early adopters of Rust since 2018 and a lot of our infra, voice tech, and even some of the current client is already Rust, the holy grail was getting the whole client there. That means Electron goes away, and so does React Native, mobile keeps native UI but shares app… https://t.co/2CgWyOzaq0 pic.twitter.com/IdOGd4nUgl

Instead, the mobile app would retain its native user interface while sharing application code with the desktop version through Rust.

He also clarified that the new desktop client would not use Tauri, another framework commonly associated with Rust-based applications, but would instead rely on GPUI.

Alongside the announcement, Vishnevskiy shared a screenshot of Windows Task Manager showing an application labeled “Discord Phoenix” using approximately 290 MB of RAM.

The screenshot also showed Google Chrome using roughly 1.57 GB of memory, Spotify consuming 653 MB, and Steam Client WebHelper using 856 MB.

Discord testing new “Game Mode” feature to help your PC run better

Discord doubles Nitro upload limit to 1GB alongside server organization features

Discord rolls out huge batch of highly requested features after asking users for ideas

In a follow-up post, Discord revealed just how much faster the new app loads on desktop.

“On the left is the Discord you use daily. And on the right is a new version we’re working on, rebuilt in Rust,” they said.

On the left is the Discord you use daily. And on the right is a new version we're working on, rebuilt in Rust https://t.co/K4WnggdmEs

While the image suggests the experimental Discord client can operate with a relatively small memory footprint, it does not establish how much RAM the current Discord app would use under identical conditions.

The rewrite is not Discord’s only effort to reduce its impact on PC performance. In September 2026, the company began testing a new Game Mode designed to automatically reduce animations and disable visual effects while gaming, lowering CPU and GPU usage.

Unlike Game Mode, which focuses on reducing resource consumption during gameplay, the move to Rust would change the underlying technology powering Discord itself. However, the company has yet to reveal when the rewritten app will become available to the public.

#10721. 7 Engineering Patterns for Measuring Traffic From AI Search and Chat Tools

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

More visitors now arrive from chat assistants and AI answer boxes, but many analytics setups still lump them into "direct" or "referral". Teams then argue about whether AI search matters, using numbers that cannot answer the question.

Measuring this traffic is an engineering task. You need to capture the referrer, classify it, store it safely and know where the data is blind. This article covers seven patterns, including a small classifier you can run.

Explicit tags are more reliable than guessing from a referrer. If you control a link, such as a partner mention or a newsletter, add a standard utm_source and record it on landing. SitePoint's tutorial on building a campaign attribution tracking system covers capturing UTM parameters, storing first-touch and last-touch data, and keeping conversions with no attribution marked as unattributed. Tagged visits should always win over inferred ones.

Browsers limit what they send. MDN's reference for the Referrer-Policy header explains that the default, strict-origin-when-cross-origin, sends only the origin for cross-origin requests over HTTPS and sends no referrer when moving from HTTPS to HTTP.

Keep the classification logic in one place, with a list of known sources that you can update. This function checks for a campaign tag first, then falls back to the referrer hostname, and labels missing referrers as direct or unknown:

The domain list will change as tools appear and rename themselves, so review it regularly. The exact-match check also prevents a lookalike domain such as notchatgpt.com from being counted.

Save the raw classification inputs, the referrer origin and the campaign tag, next to the result. When the domain list changes, you can reclassify old data. Keep raw events for a limited time and aggregated numbers longer. Avoid storing full IP addresses or fingerprints, since you do not need them for this question.

Analytics can show that visits arrive, but explaining why a brand appears in an AI answer, or what to change in content, is a separate specialty. Compare any outside recommendation with the traffic you can measure yourself.

A good report states what it cannot see. Many AI answers are read without a click, some visits carry no referrer, and Search Console reports AI feature clicks together with other web results. Put those limits at the top of the dashboard. A number with its caveats is more useful than a confident chart that hides them.

Can I identify every visit that comes from an AI tool?

No. Some tools send a referrer and some do not, so your numbers will undercount. Use campaign tags wherever you control the link.

Should I use UTM parameters for AI traffic?

Only where you control the link. You cannot tag a link that a chat tool generates on its own.

Keep it only as long as you need to reclassify and audit, for example about 30 days, and keep aggregated metrics longer.

Measuring AI search traffic comes down to honest data handling: define your questions, prefer explicit campaign tags, understand the limits of the referrer, classify visits in one tested function, store auditable events, bring in specialist advice where you need it, and report the blind spots. The classifier above is short, but it makes the logic explicit so you can review and improve it as new tools appear.

#10720. Viral Red Baron worker pauses $787K fundraiser as he steps away from spotlight

Red Baron employee Walter E. Zerod has announced he’s pausing donations to his viral GoFundMe, which has raised over $787,000, as he looks to step away from the spotlight and spend time with his family.

The father of four became an internet sensation in late October after a video showed him confronting an Instagram prankster who pretended to steal money from him while he was stocking a grocery store freezer.

During the confrontation, Walt explained that he was struggling to pay his mortgage while working long hours to support his children.

The footage sparked an outpouring of support, with homeless veteran Luke Oakenshield launching a fundraiser that has since collected more than $787,000 from over 22,000 donations.

However, in a November 5 update on his GoFundMe, Walt announced that he was bringing the fundraising effort to a close and would no longer be making public statements.

“Your kind words have meant the world to my family and I this past week. I still cannot believe how much you have all rallied behind us, and I can never thank you enough,” he wrote.

“I’ve been able to spend lots of extra time at home with my family this week.”

Despite previously considering interviews to share his story, Walt revealed that he’s decided against making any media appearances.

He also confirmed that donations would be paused on Thursday, November 5, exactly one week after the internet began rallying behind him.

Internet rallies behind Red Baron worker who snapped at Instagram prankster

GoFundMe launched for homeless veteran who raised $500,000 for Red Baron worker

DoorDash customer finds Dasher in car crash & helps raise $15K to get him back on the road

“If you have the means and would like to continue helping others, please consider supporting another fundraiser, a local charity, or a church helping families in need this holiday season,” he added.

Walt also gave an update on his friendship with Oakenshield, who received his own GoFundMe after supporters discovered he was a homeless veteran living out of his car.

“I’ve also stayed in touch with Luke, and I look forward to continuing that friendship as he navigates all the blessings that have come his way.”

Walt concluded by announcing that this would be his final public update as he prepares to spend the holiday season with his family.

“Thank you for your kindness, your generosity, and for making my family feel so supported. We will never forget it.”

#10718. Hackers target blood banks by setting freezers to a boiling 230 degrees

Hackers have targeted blood banks in France by programming freezers storing blood plasma to reach a staggering 110C (230F), following a wave of similar cyberattacks on supermarkets across Europe.

The cyberattack struck three cold-storage facilities operated by the French Blood Establishment (EFS) on November 2, with attackers reportedly attempting to raise temperatures from their normal -30C (-22F) to well above boiling point.

According to The Independent, the attack was detected before any blood products were damaged, preventing what could have been a devastating loss of medical supplies.

The incident comes just days after hackers targeted supermarket fridges across Europe, forcing retailers to throw away large quantities of spoiled food.

French publication Le Canard Enchaîné first reported the attack, revealing that hackers had reprogrammed refrigeration equipment used to store plasma intended for transfusions and medical treatments.

“Temperatures and defrosting thresholds were raised to extremely high levels,” EFS confirmed in a statement.

Fortunately, the facility’s monitoring and alarm systems detected the suspicious changes before the freezers could reach the programmed temperatures.

“No health consequences have been identified, and no blood products were lost,” EFS said.

According to the Associated Press, staff were able to secure or relocate the affected plasma, allowing blood collection and distribution services to continue without interruption.

The attack reportedly involved equipment supplied by refrigeration company Coolworld, which blamed the security vulnerability on a component from a third-party supplier.

French cybersecurity authorities and the country’s Health Ministry are investigating the incident. It remains unclear whether the attack is directly connected to the supermarket incidents or who was responsible.

Supermarket fridges hacked again as cyberattack turns them up to 122 degrees

Hackers turn supermarket fridges up to 122 degrees forcing stores to throw away food

Chinese cyber criminals hack Staples to steal millions in gift cards as part of $100M crime spree

The attempted sabotage follows an October cyberattack that saw supermarket freezers reach 122F, destroying food supplies at hundreds of stores in France.

The damage has been substantial. Dutch supermarket operator Ahold Delhaize warned that the earlier attacks could reduce its fourth-quarter sales by as much as €250 million.

The growing threat has also caught the attention of US authorities. On November 5, the FBI and Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency warned of ongoing attacks against refrigeration systems, including the potential for spoiled inventory and fires.

#10715. Astrocade launches $100K contest to vibe code games using AI

Astrocade is launching a $100,000 creator competition, challenging 25 creators to produce viral playable content, with the entire prize going to whoever attracts the most plays.

Selected creators will spend three weeks over this holiday period developing interactive experiences using Astrocade’s AI-powered creation tools.

Unlike traditional game development, Astrocade allows users to create playable content simply by describing their ideas in natural language, meaning no coding or game development experience is required.

The platform is looking for creators who understand what makes content go viral, whether that’s memes, pranks, inside jokes, or everyday moments turned into interactive experiences.

Applications for the competition are open from November 5 until November 20, with 25 creators selected to compete for the $100,000 prize.

Each participant will have three weeks, from November 30 to December 20, to create content on the platform. They can submit multiple games too, with the winner determined by the total number of plays across all their published content during the competition.

And the winner-take-all format means one creator will walk away with the full $100,000.

Astrocade’s approach is designed to put creators on an equal footing, with everyone using the same AI creation tools. Rather than technical ability, the competition focuses on creativity and understanding of what people really want to play.

The platform works similarly to a social media feed, but replaces posts, videos, and images with interactive experiences that you can play instantly.

Creators can also earn money from their content outside the competition through Astrocade’s existing play-based monetization program, meaning successful creations could continue generating revenue after the contest ends.

The announcement comes as Astrocade reports significant growth: According to figures shared by the company, they reached 10 million monthly active players in August 2026, doubling its audience in just four months.

What users call a “fancy font” is often not a font at all. The text may contain Unicode characters from blocks such as Mathematical Alphanumeric Symbols.

The solution is not simply “normalize everything”.

Normalization and text segmentation solve different problems.

Many Unicode bugs stay invisible until a user enters accented text, emoji, combining marks, mathematical symbols, or another writing system.

Styled Unicode text uses separate Unicode characters that visually resemble bold, italic, script, monospace, or other letter styles.

Unlike CSS typography, the appearance is encoded partly in the characters themselves.

Because visually similar strings may contain different Unicode code points.

It is often useful for search, matching, or certain identifiers, but it may be destructive for text that should preserve the user's original appearance.

For display content, preserve the original.

If your application needs normalized search or matching, consider storing or generating a separate searchable representation.

They are better when your requirement is genuinely Unicode-aware.

For example, \p{Letter} can match letters from many writing systems.

That does not mean every matched character should automatically be allowed in security-sensitive identifiers.

Normalization can collapse some equivalent or compatibility forms, but visually confusable characters across scripts require separate identifier and security policies.

The biggest Unicode mistake is not using the wrong JavaScript method.

It is giving every string in your application the same rules.

A search index is not the original content.

A character counter is not a storage limit.

Once you separate those responsibilities, styled Unicode becomes much easier to handle.

Normalize what the system needs to match.

Restrict what must function as a secure identifier.

Segment what the interface needs to count.

And before shipping, paste something stranger than “Hello world” into the form.

That small habit catches an surprising number of text bugs before your users do.

#10710. Drinkable Street Fighter trading cards have baffled fans predicting Pokemon & Yu-Gi-Oh versions

Japan has somehow found a way to combine trading cards and energy drinks, and the internet can’t quite believe what it’s seeing.

A bizarre Japanese TV segment has gone viral after showcasing drinkable trading cards featuring characters from Capcom’s Street Fighter 6.

Yes, drinkable trading cards. And no, that doesn’t mean putting cardboard in a blender.

The segment, which highlighted products predicted to become popular in 2027, featured presenters demonstrating the unusual creation by bending cards in half and drinking liquid directly from the packaging.

The footage has taken social media by storm, with one upload alone accumulating over 15 million views on X.

A Japanese news show featured drinkable trading cards in its ranking of possible hit products for 2027. Each card contains 12ml of an energy drink and the card/drink company already has a collab with Capcom's Street Fighter. pic.twitter.com/XufheWvDvB

The product, called Energy Arts, was developed by Japanese confectionery company UHA Mikakuto in collaboration with Kindai University.

Each card contains 12ml of a concentrated, caffeine-free energy drink. Rather than tearing open a packet, users simply fold the card until a small opening appears, allowing them to suck out the liquid.

The cards feature 24 different Street Fighter 6 designs, including recognizable fighters such as Ryu, E. Honda, Dhalsim, and Jamie.

According to the manufacturer’s announcement, each serving contains 1,000mg of arginine and 1,000mg of citrulline, two amino acids commonly used in supplements.

The idea is to let gamers replenish their energy without interrupting a match. UHA Mikakuto even claims the process takes just half a second, which is apparently enough time to squeeze in a drink between rounds.

The company also promotes the tiny servings as a way to reduce bathroom breaks during lengthy gaming sessions. Because nothing ruins a competitive Street Fighter match quite like needing to use the toilet.

Pokemon cards can now be delivered in 15 minutes with massive discounts on rare cards

Interestingly, the cards aren’t actually new. As Dexerto previously reported, they were first unveiled in January 2026 before becoming available through Japanese retailers in July.

However, their appearance on Japanese television has given the unusual collaboration a second wave of attention, with the cards appearing fifth in a ranking of products expected to take off in 2027.

Some users expect other brands to join the trend, such as Yu-Gi-Oh. “I activate Pot of Greed which allows me to take a sip of 2 energy drinks inside this card,” one joked.

“Can’t wait for Pokemon drinkable trading cards,” another chimed in.

Some expressed concern about scalping if other IPs like Pokemon got involved, while others weren’t convinced drinkable cards were a good idea to begin with.

Of course, there’s one glaring problem for collectors: actually drinking the energy shot means bending the card in half, potentially ruining the very collectible you wanted to preserve.

For anyone hoping to keep their favorite fighter in mint condition, it might be worth buying two. One for the collection and another for when you desperately need 12ml of Street Fighter juice.

#10706. Man fighting to keep badger he nursed back to health after officials reject license

A Scottish man is fighting to keep a badger named Harriet after saving her from starvation, only for wildlife officials to tell him she must be released into the wild or sent to a zoo.

Graeme Wilson, a 55-year-old ecologist from the Scottish Borders, rescued Harriet in April after the young badger was discovered severely underweight and filthy inside a cattle trough, roughly 300 feet from her sett.

Wilson, who operates a wildlife rescue and rehabilitation service called GW Ecology, took Harriet in and nursed her back to health.

However, he quickly noticed something unusual about the animal. Despite being just a few months old, Harriet appeared remarkably comfortable drinking milk from a bottle, leading him to suspect she had previously been raised by humans.

“It was almost second nature when she saw the bottle,” Wilson told the BBC.

“I have cared for injured badgers before and never have I seen something like it. It was clear then she couldn’t be released back into the wild.”

Wilson reportedly attempted to release Harriet at two different badger setts, but she became extremely distressed and appeared determined to return to him.

Unfortunately, keeping Harriet has now become a legal battle.

According to PEOPLE, Scotland’s wildlife agency, NatureScot, rejected Wilson’s application for an educational license that would allow him to continue caring for Harriet.

Officials instead advised that the badger should be released or transferred to a licensed zoo, something Wilson believes could put her welfare at risk.

Sewer-dwelling man arrested for harassing woman’s children

Bear finally freed by rescuers after getting head stuck in giant stove pipe

Deer put down after attacking man in London park as feeding blamed

“Badgers are companion animals, they are a social animal and unfortunately for Harriet she has decided that humans are her social group,” he explained.

“Can you imagine Harriet approaching someone on a dog walk or in the street? There is only one way that would end.”

He also fears that sending Harriet to a zoo would leave her lonely and distressed.

“Harriet’s upbringing means she needs human interaction, not to be put behind glass and stared at,” Wilson said.

NatureScot has defended its decision, explaining that his application failed to meet the legal requirements for keeping a protected wild animal.

However, the agency clarified that Wilson could allow Harriet to roam freely from his property while continuing to provide food and shelter, provided her movements are not restricted.

The organization says discussions are ongoing to find a solution that prioritizes Harriet’s welfare.

Meanwhile, a GoFundMe campaign has been launched to support her care and potentially fund a specially designed habitat if Wilson receives permission to keep her.

The unusual dispute echoes the controversy surrounding Peanut the squirrel, who was seized from his owner by New York wildlife officials in 2024.

For now, Wilson remains determined to give Harriet a safe future.

“Harriet never asked for any of this — she deserves to live happily,” he said.

#10704. 9 Checks Before Shipping a Product Email: A Workflow for Developers and Designers

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

A product email can look correct in a design file and still fail its reader. The primary action may disappear when images are blocked. A long workspace name may break the layout. A staging link may survive into production. Even when the message renders correctly, the application may send it twice.

These failures cross design, frontend, backend, and delivery boundaries. A useful release process checks each boundary independently and records what the tests actually establish.

This article uses a workspace invitation as an example. The recipient needs to understand who invited them, identify the workspace, and open a valid acceptance link. The same workflow applies to account notifications, activity summaries, and many other product emails.

Write a short behavioral contract before designing the template:

This separates visual preferences from required behavior. A rounded button is a design choice; a usable invitation link is a requirement.

Build fixtures for a short workspace name, a long name, an accented inviter name, missing optional information, and a translated version. Use synthetic recipients and tokens.

Designers should review these fixtures early. A layout approved only with ideal copy leaves developers to invent overflow behavior later.

MJML provides email-oriented components that compile to responsive HTML. React Email offers a component-based workflow suited to teams already using React.

Choose according to the team’s maintenance needs. Introducing both usually adds complexity without helping a single template.

Regardless of authoring tool, review the generated HTML. The compiled document is what the sending pipeline passes onward, and it can differ substantially from the source component.

Check that the output contains the expected heading, action URL, image alternatives, language information, and footer. Confirm that production rendering uses the same dependency versions as the reviewed build.

SitePoint’s HTML email coding guide provides useful background on email markup. Treat older examples as starting points and verify compatibility against the clients your audience actually uses.

Avoid adding application JavaScript to an email template. Put interactive workflows on a web page and use the email to explain and link to the next action.

Browser support and email-client support are different things. A layout working in Chrome does not establish that it works in every Outlook or Gmail environment.

Use Can I Email to investigate the HTML and CSS features your design depends on. Read the support notes and test dates, not only the headline support percentage.

Define a small client matrix using available audience evidence. Record the specific client and platform; “Outlook” alone is too broad to describe a test environment.

For the invitation example, the baseline should preserve:

SitePoint’s HTML email tips and tricks offers additional implementation context.

Design the baseline first. Decorative effects can improve the experience, but they should not carry information that disappears when a client ignores a CSS rule.

Use visible text for the essential message. A large image containing the entire invitation fails when images are unavailable and gives readers less control over text presentation.

Give meaningful images appropriate alternatives, and use empty alternative text for purely decorative images. Choose descriptive link labels such as “Accept your workspace invitation” instead of repeating “Click here.”

Two useful tools address different questions:

Neither establishes accessibility across every email client. A client may modify markup or colors after delivery.

Manually inspect reading order, text enlargement, keyboard access to links, and the message with images unavailable. Check the delivered email with relevant assistive technology when that is part of your supported environment.

For dark mode, examine the actual resulting colors. Changing a browser preview’s preferred color scheme does not reproduce every email client’s color transformations.

A template preview tests the template. It does not verify that the application selects the right recipient, subject, language, or invitation token.

Route development email to Mailpit, a local SMTP testing tool, and trigger the real application flow using synthetic data.

Mailpit also provides HTML compatibility and link-checking features. Review what a link checker will request before using it on action URLs. An automated request should not consume a single-use invitation or trigger a state-changing action.

A successful capture proves that the development application generated a message. It does not prove that a production mailbox provider will accept it or place it in the inbox.

A perfectly rendered email with a localhost link is still broken.

For a specific invitation flow, an explicit destination validator can catch common mistakes before rendering. The following example assumes invitations must use HTTPS, a single approved hostname, an exact path, and a token:

Run this standalone example with node --test invitation-url.test.mjs. Replace the hostname and route with your application’s documented contract before integrating it.

This checks URL shape, not token authenticity, expiry, or authorization. The receiving application must enforce those properties.

Apply the validator before inserting the URL into a template, and use context-appropriate escaping during rendering. Inspect the final delivered link too, because a sending provider may rewrite it for tracking.

Playwright is useful for repeatable checks against a rendered HTML preview. Test narrow widths, long content, missing optional fields, and the presence of essential text and links.

A browser test can assert that the action has the expected accessible name and destination. It can also capture screenshots for human review.

Keep the limitation explicit: browser automation does not emulate an email client’s HTML rewriting or all of its rendering behavior.

Use an email-client testing service such as Litmus, or controlled test accounts in the clients you support, to inspect the delivered result. Include light and dark appearances where relevant.

Record the template version and fixture alongside each preview. Otherwise, a designer and developer may approve screenshots from different builds.

Do not accept screenshot updates automatically. A changed image may reveal a genuine regression, including truncated text or a button that no longer looks actionable.

Email generation often happens in a background job. That means the release process must account for retries and partial failures.

Give the business event a stable identifier. Record which invitation event produced which send attempt, and use your queue or provider’s documented deduplication mechanisms where available.

Do not promise exactly-once sending merely because a database flag says “sent.” A crash between provider acceptance and saving that flag creates an ambiguous state.

Preserve enough event history to investigate that ambiguity without logging raw invitation tokens. Also separate “accepted by the sending provider” from “delivered to the receiving system,” and from “seen by the user.”

Rendering quality and delivery behavior require separate evidence. Review authentication, bounce handling, complaint signals, suppression behavior, and provider feedback before increasing production volume.

Start with the relevant mailbox provider’s requirements. For example, Gmail’s sender guidelines explain authentication and other requirements, with additional obligations for bulk senders. Check the requirements for your actual sending pattern rather than treating one checklist as universal.

For vendor research at this stage, treat vendor-published comparisons as vendor-authored material: evaluate their claims against provider policies and your own delivery evidence.

Warmup activity is not a substitute for appropriate recipient expectations, correct authentication, or operational monitoring. It also cannot establish that a template is accessible or that an invitation token is valid.

Choose tools according to the question being investigated. A compatibility lookup explains feature support; an SMTP capture shows message construction; a client preview shows rendering; provider events describe delivery outcomes. Keeping those responsibilities clear makes failures easier to diagnose.

A release is ready when the team can explain what the message does, demonstrate the important failure cases, and identify which evidence supports each conclusion.

#10702. Dragon Ball Daima censored in France to erase Mr Popo, but fans can still hear him

Dragon Ball Daima has completely removed Mr. Popo from the screen in France, with the character being edited out of scenes despite his voice remaining in the anime.

The latest installment in Akira Toriyama’s iconic franchise originally debuted in October 2024, following Goku and his allies as they’re transformed into children and forced to venture into the Demon Realm.

On November 4, 2026, Daima made its French television debut on Gulli, but viewers quickly noticed that one familiar character was nowhere to be seen.

As reported by Journal du Geek, Mr. Popo, the longtime attendant of Kami and later Dende, had been completely erased from the screen.

Rather than simply cutting his dialogue, scenes featuring the character were removed, cropped, or edited to ensure he never appeared on camera.

Strangely enough, however, his voice can still be heard in certain scenes, meaning the character technically still exists in the French version.

Mr Popo a été supprimé de Dragon Ball Daima en France ! Il parle, mais n'apparait pas à l'image !! LA HONTE 😑@ToeiAnimationEU … Non mais sérieux…. pic.twitter.com/h1z5nxseaL

“Mr. Popo has been removed from Dragon Ball Daima in France! He speaks, but doesn’t appear on screen!” one furious fan wrote on X.

Another report indicated that Episode 2 received similar treatment, with scenes heavily re-edited and zoomed in to hide Mr. Popo.

The character’s design has been controversial for decades, with critics arguing that his dark skin, exaggerated red lips, and other features resemble racist caricatures.

EN FRANCE, LE PERSONNAGE DE MR POPO DANS L’ANIME DRAGON BALL : DAIMA A ÉTÉ CENSURÉ ! ❌La voix du personnage est présente dans les épisodes, mais il n’apparaît pas à l’écran. pic.twitter.com/bHBkeZXHex

However, defenders of the design argue that Mr. Popo was never intended to represent a black person.

Fans have pointed to similarities with Mahakala, a dark-skinned guardian deity in Buddhist and Hindu traditions, suggesting his appearance draws from religious imagery rather than racist stereotypes.

Dragon Ball Daima episode one anime details leak ahead of 2024 release

Dragon Ball Daima divides fans with new character designs

This isn’t even the first time Dragon Ball has censored him. In the American CW broadcast of Dragon Ball Z Kai in 2010, Mr. Popo was famously recolored blue.

France also isn’t the first country to remove him from Daima. Germany’s broadcast received similar edits when the anime premiered on Toggo Plus in August 2026.

It’s currently unclear whether the French censorship was ordered by Gulli or Toei Animation Europe, and neither has publicly confirmed the reason behind the changes.

The controversy is particularly notable given Toriyama’s involvement in Daima’s story and character designs, with the anime even offering new clues about Mr. Popo’s mysterious origins.

For fans wanting to see the original version, all 20 episodes of Dragon Ball Daima are available uncensored with subtitles on streaming services including Crunchyroll and Netflix in France.

The promotion provides up to $40 in total savings, with each order requiring a minimum purchase of $25 before taxes and fees.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Most identity theft online starts with a password. Someone reuses one, a site gets breached, a fake login page collects a few more, and suddenly a stranger is inside an email account resetting everything else.

Passkeys are the industry’s attempt to remove that weak link. Apple, Google, and Microsoft all support them now, and plenty of big sites already offer them at sign-in. But do they actually make identity theft harder, or do they just move the problem somewhere else?

The honest answer is a bit of both. This article looks at how passkeys work under the hood, which attacks they shut down, which ones they don’t touch, and what you need to get right if you’re adding them to your own site.

Passwords have one basic flaw. They’re a shared secret. You know it, the server knows it (or a hash of it), and anyone who gets a copy can use it from anywhere.

That one flaw feeds most of the account takeover attacks you hear about:

Two-factor authentication helps, but not as much as people think. SMS codes can be intercepted or stolen through SIM swaps. One-time codes from an app can still be phished, because a fake site can simply ask for the code and pass it along in real time.

A passkey is a pair of cryptographic keys made for one specific website. It’s built on the WebAuthn standard from the W3C and the FIDO Alliance.

Here’s the short version of what happens:

Nothing secret ever crosses the network, and nothing secret is stored on the server. That small change has big consequences.

This is the biggest win. Every passkey is tied to the domain it was created for. Your browser won’t use a passkey for example.com on examp1e-login.com, no matter how real the page looks. That protection only holds if the attacker can’t fall back to a password or a weak recovery path, which is why the rollout advice later in this article matters.

With a password, the user is the one who has to spot the fake. With a passkey, the browser checks the domain for them. People get tired and click bad links. The browser doesn’t.

Each passkey is unique to one site, so there’s nothing to reuse. An attacker can’t take a passkey from one breach and try it somewhere else, because there’s no shared value to try.

If an attacker dumps a site’s database, they get public keys. A public key can check a signature, but it can’t make one. So the stolen data can’t be used to sign in as anyone.

This doesn’t make a breach harmless (more on that below), but it does remove the part that usually leads straight to account takeovers.

This is where a lot of articles get too optimistic. Passkeys protect the login step. Identity theft is a much bigger problem than that.

Every site needs a way back in for people who lose their phone. If that recovery path is an SMS code, an email link, or a support agent who can be talked into resetting things, attackers will go after that instead.

A site with passkeys and a weak recovery flow is only as strong as the recovery flow. This is the part developers most often underestimate. The OWASP Forgot Password Cheat Sheet is a good checklist for hardening it.

A breach that exposes names, addresses, birth dates, or government ID numbers is still a breach. Criminals don’t need to log in to your accounts to open new ones in your name. They can apply for credit, file fake tax returns, or run scams with that data alone.

Passkeys do nothing about this kind of identity theft. It’s why credit monitoring, freezes, and alert services are still worth knowing about even when your logins are locked down. If you want a broader look at how those tools compare, these theft protection insights from Cybernews cover what different services actually monitor.

Someone can still call a person, pretend to be their bank, and talk them into approving something. Passkeys make that harder because there’s no code to read out loud, but scammers adapt. User education still matters.

The good news is that the browser side is fairly small. Most of the real work happens on the server. The MDN guide to the Web Authentication API covers every option in detail, and the Passkeys Developer Resources site is a good source for implementation guidance.

Here’s a stripped-down registration call. In a real app, the challenge and user ID come from your server, never from the browser.

A couple of details worth noticing. The rp.id is what ties the passkey to your domain, so set it to the domain users actually sign in on. And user.id should be a random value rather than an email, since it’s stored on the user’s device.

Passkeys feel best when they show up right in the username field’s autofill menu. This is called conditional UI, and it lets you add passkeys without changing your login form much.

Users who have a passkey see it in the dropdown. Users who don’t can keep typing a password like before. That makes a gradual rollout much easier.

Verifying WebAuthn responses means checking the challenge, the origin, the relying party ID, and the signature. It’s very easy to get one of those subtly wrong. Use a well-maintained library instead of writing it yourself. SimpleWebAuthn is a popular choice for Node.js, and most major languages have solid options.

One thing that trips people up: signature counters. Older hardware keys increment a counter on every use, and some guides tell you to reject sign-ins if it goes backward. Synced passkeys often just report zero, so a strict counter check can lock out real users.

A few practical tips from teams that have already done this:

There’s also the question of moving passkeys between platforms. Early on, passkeys stuck to one ecosystem, which annoyed a lot of people. Password managers like 1Password and Bitwarden now store and sync them across platforms, and the FIDO Alliance has published specifications for moving passkeys and other credentials between providers, the Credential Exchange Format and its companion protocol. It’s getting better, but it’s worth telling users where their passkeys live.

Yes, and by a lot, for one specific part of the problem.

Passkeys close off phishing, credential stuffing, and password database leaks, which are the most common ways criminals take over accounts. That alone makes them one of the most meaningful security upgrades the web has seen in years.

But identity theft is bigger than logins. Weak recovery flows, stolen sessions, and leaked personal data all still lead to real harm, and passkeys don’t fix any of them on their own.

If you’re building for the web, treat passkeys as a strong foundation, not the whole house. Add them, make recovery just as solid, keep your sessions protected, and collect as little personal data as you can. That combination does far more for your users than any single feature.

#10688. The Privacy Risks of Browser Extensions: What Developers Should Know

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

The extension a developer installed three years ago can probably read everything they do in the browser today.

General online security advice from VPNpro and similar guides cover the network side of staying safe, but they cannot see what an extension does inside the browser. That layer is more the developer's responsibility. The risk is complicated, but the fix is simple: request fewer permissions, narrower host access, and less data, and review every update. Here is a walkthrough of each.

Think about what a developer has open on a normal day: a cloud console, a staging dashboard, a private repo, maybe webmail. One over-permissioned extension sees all of it.

The most common mistake is asking for broad access early and planning to trim it later. Later rarely arrives.

A manifest like this should raise eyebrows:

A developer who cannot justify a permission in a short sentence likely shouldn't include the permission in the build.

Host permissions deserve their own attention because they define how far the extension can reach. A few habits make a real difference:

This also helps adoption. People hesitate when an extension asks to read every site they visit. A narrow request looks, and is, more trustworthy.

Analytics and error logging are where good intentions leak. A crash report that includes the full page URL may contain a session token in the query string. A “usage event” may capture page titles from internal tools.

The most secure approach is to collect only the data a feature needs and to process the data locally if possible. When data has to be sent, it should be stripped down to the absolute minimum. Avoid sending query strings, and truncate URLs to the domain name where possible. Never send page content if it is not absolutely necessary.

Remote code is another trap. Manifest V3 restricts remotely hosted code for a good reason. A script fetched at runtime can modify its behavior after the fact, and one can’t audit what it will do in the future. Bundle everything and the code that is reviewed will be identical to the code that is run.

A good extension today can become a risky one next year. Two patterns keep repeating.

Ownership changes. Popular extensions get sold, and the new owner ships an update with tracking or worse. The Great Suspender, a widely used tab tool, ended up flagged as malware after a change of hands.

Compromised publisher accounts. If an attacker phishes the developer account, they can push a malicious update to every existing user. Cyberhaven’s extension was hit by a phished administrator account in late December 2024.

The defenses are mostly boring, which is a good sign. Hardware-key two-factor authentication on the publisher account, a short list of people allowed to publish, and a review step before each release stops most of it. Lockfiles, pinned versions and regular dependency audits cover the code side.

Teams that only install extensions can apply the same thinking. Keep an approved list, review updates that change permissions, and remove anything nobody uses. Following security news is worthwhile too, since incidents involving popular extensions tend to be reported publicly.

It is only one layer, though. A VPN protects traffic in transit. It does nothing about an add-on that reads page content inside the browser, so it never replaces a proper permission review.

Simpler habits do more here. A separate browser profile for development keeps test extensions away from personal accounts. Fake or low-privilege accounts for testing avoid exposing real credentials. And installers for any tool, VPN clients included, should come from the official site or store, never from a mirror.

Safe extensions come down to restraint. Ask for less access, collect less data, send less off the device, and explain more to the user. Developers who treat every permission as a liability end up with extensions people can trust, and teams that review what they install avoid the worst surprises.

#10681. “Existential risk” – Why scientists are racing to define consciousness

As artificial intelligence continues to advance and ethical concerns grow alongside it, scientists say the need to understand consciousness has reached a critical point.

In a new review published in Frontiers in Science, researchers warn that progress in AI and neurotechnology is moving faster than scientific understanding of consciousness. This gap, they argue, could lead to serious ethical problems if it is not addressed.

The authors say explaining how consciousness emerges is now an urgent scientific and moral priority. A clearer understanding could eventually make it possible to develop scientific methods for detecting consciousness. That breakthrough would have far-reaching consequences for AI development, prenatal policy, animal welfare, medicine, mental health care, law, and emerging technologies such as brain-computer interfaces.

"Consciousness science is no longer a purely philosophical pursuit. It has real implications for every facet of society -- and for understanding what it means to be human," said lead author Prof Axel Cleeremans from Université Libre de Bruxelles. "Understanding consciousness is one of the most substantial challenges of 21st-century science -- and it's now urgent due to advances in AI and other technologies.

"If we become able to create consciousness -- even accidentally -- it would raise immense ethical challenges and even existential risk," added Cleeremans, a European Research Council (ERC) grantee.

Consciousness, commonly described as awareness of both the world around us and ourselves, remains one of science's most difficult puzzles. Despite decades of research, scientists still lack agreement on how subjective experience emerges from biological processes.

Researchers have identified brain regions and neural activity linked to conscious experience, but major disagreements remain. Scientists continue to debate which brain systems are truly necessary for consciousness and how they interact to produce awareness. Some researchers even question whether this approach captures the problem correctly.

The new review examines the current state of consciousness science, future directions for the field, and the possible consequences if humans succeed in fully explaining or even creating consciousness. This includes the possibility of consciousness emerging in machines or in lab-grown brain-like systems known as "brain organoids."

The authors argue that developing evidence-based tests for consciousness could transform how awareness is identified across many contexts. Such tools could help detect consciousness in patients with brain injuries or dementia and determine when awareness arises in fetuses, animals, brain organoids, or even AI systems.

While this would represent a major scientific advance, the researchers caution that it would also create difficult ethical and legal questions. Determining that a system is conscious would force society to reconsider how that system should be treated.

"Progress in consciousness science will reshape how we see ourselves and our relationship to both artificial intelligence and the natural world," said co-author Prof Anil Seth from the University of Sussex and ERC grantee. "The question of consciousness is ancient -- but it's never been more urgent than now."

A deeper understanding of consciousness could have wide-ranging effects across society.

In medicine, it could improve care for patients who are unresponsive and assumed to be unconscious. Measurements inspired by integrated information theory and global workspace theory[1] have already detected signs of awareness in some individuals diagnosed with unresponsive wakefulness syndrome. Further progress could refine these tools to better assess consciousness in coma, advanced dementia, and anesthesia, and influence treatment decisions and end-of-life care.

Mental health treatment could also benefit. Understanding the biological basis of subjective experience may help researchers develop better therapies for conditions such as depression, anxiety, and schizophrenia by narrowing the gap between animal studies and human emotional experience.

Greater insight into consciousness could reshape how humans think about their moral responsibilities toward animals. Identifying which animals and systems are sentient could influence animal research practices, farming, food consumption, and conservation strategies. "Understanding the nature of consciousness in particular animals would transform how we treat them and emerging biological systems that are being synthetically generated by scientists," said co-author Prof Liad Mudrik from Tel Aviv University and ERC grantee.

Consciousness research could also affect how the legal system understands responsibility. New findings may challenge traditional legal concepts such as mens rea, the "guilty mind" required to establish intent. As neuroscience reveals how much behavior arises from unconscious processes, courts may need to reconsider where responsibility begins and ends.

At the same time, advances in AI, brain organoids, and brain-computer interfaces raise the possibility of creating or altering awareness beyond natural biological limits. While some researchers believe consciousness might arise through computation alone, others argue that biological factors play an essential role. "Even if 'conscious AI' is impossible using standard digital computers, AI that gives the impression of being conscious raises many societal and ethical challenges," said Seth.

The authors emphasize the need for a coordinated, evidence-based approach to studying consciousness. One proposed strategy involves adversarial collaborations, in which competing theories are tested against each other through experiments designed jointly by their supporters. "We need more team science to break theoretical silos and overcome existing biases and assumptions," said Mudrik. "This step has the potential to move the field forward."

The researchers also argue that scientific work should place greater emphasis on phenomenology (what consciousness feels like) alongside studies of function (what consciousness does).

"Cooperative efforts are essential to make progress -- and to ensure society is prepared for the ethical, medical, and technological consequences of understanding, and perhaps creating, consciousness," said Cleeremans.

#10679. Browser Fingerprinting Explained: How Websites Identify You and How Developers Can Reduce It

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Most articles on this topic stop at the scary part. This one is written for people who build websites, so we’ll go a bit further: what goes into a fingerprint, what the collection code actually looks like, and what you can change in your own projects.

Think of a fingerprint as a stack of clues rather than a single value. Your time zone is shared by millions of people. So is your screen resolution. Put twenty clues like that together, though, and the crowd shrinks fast.

Here’s roughly where the clues come from.

HTTP headers. Before any JavaScript runs, every request already tells the server a lot. The User-Agent string and the Accept-Language header give away your browser, its version, your OS, and your languages. Chromium browsers also send Client Hints.

JavaScript APIs. Plenty of everyday APIs leak device details. screen.width and screen.height, navigator.hardwareConcurrency (your CPU core count), navigator.deviceMemory (Chromium only), navigator.platform, and your time zone all add something. Plugin lists used to be a goldmine, but modern browsers now return a fixed, generic list, so that one’s mostly dead.

Rendering. This is the clever bit. Ask two computers to draw the exact same text, and the pixels won’t match perfectly. Fonts, graphics drivers, and the GPU itself all nudge the output slightly. Same browser, same version, different hardware, different result.

Network details. Your IP address, connection type, and even the way your browser sets up a TLS connection can help. IPs change, so these clues are less reliable. Trackers mostly use them to back up a match they already suspect.

How unique does this make you? Back in 2010, the EFF’s Panopticlick study tested around 470,000 browsers and found that about 84% of them had a unique fingerprint. (The project still exists, now called Cover Your Tracks.) Later studies with bigger samples found lower numbers, especially on phones, since a lot of phones share near-identical hardware. The percentages move around, but the basic idea hasn’t changed.

Canvas fingerprinting gets talked about the most. Here’s a basic version:

Read through it and you’d never guess it was tracking code. It draws an orange box, writes some text, and exports the image. The catch is that anti-aliasing and subpixel rendering vary from device to device, so that exported string varies too.

The data URL is long and clunky, so trackers usually hash it into something shorter. With the Web Crypto API, that’s a few extra lines:

WebGL fingerprinting follows the same idea with 3D graphics. A script draws a hidden scene and also reads the WEBGL_debug_renderer_info extension, which can reveal your GPU’s make and model. Audio fingerprinting is sneakier. The script generates a sound, runs it through an AudioContext, and hashes the result. Different audio stacks produce slightly different numbers.

It’s worth remembering that the Canvas API, WebGL, and the Web Audio API were built for charts, games, and music apps. Tracking is a side effect of how much they expose. The W3C’s guidance on mitigating fingerprinting in web specifications covers how standards authors try to avoid adding new signals.

You might not write a single line of fingerprinting code yourself and still end up involved. There are three common ways that happens.

Your third-party scripts can do it without asking you. Analytics tags, ad scripts, chat widgets, social buttons. Each of them can call the same APIs your own code can. If your page loads fifteen of them, that’s fifteen possible fingerprinters. Checking what each script does has quietly become part of the job.

Browsers are closing the door. Chrome froze most of the User-Agent string and moved detailed info into Client Hints. Safari has Advanced Fingerprinting Protection. Firefox blocks known fingerprinting scripts, and Brave randomizes values returned by fingerprintable APIs. If your site depends on the old, wide-open APIs, you’re building on ground that’s shrinking every release.

Most of this comes down to one rule: collect less, and know why you’re collecting what’s left.

Search your codebase for the high-entropy stuff: canvas exports, WebGL renderer lookups, font detection, and calls to navigator.userAgentData.getHighEntropyValues(). If a feature still works without them, take them out.

In many teams, the biggest win is boring. Someone added a fingerprinting library years ago for one fraud check, nobody reviewed it since, and it’s still loading on every page. Deleting it helps more than any clever fix.

The classic User-Agent string packs browser, exact version, OS, and CPU architecture into one header. Client Hints break that apart so you only get what you ask for.

By default, Chromium browsers already send three basic hints: Sec-CH-UA, Sec-CH-UA-Mobile, and Sec-CH-UA-Platform. For most sites, that’s plenty, and you don’t need to request anything extra. If a feature really does need more detail, ask for that one hint with Accept-CH:

Skip full version numbers, architecture, and device model unless you have a real reason. Each extra hint makes your visitors a little easier to tell apart.

Keep in mind that only Chromium-based browsers support User-Agent Client Hints. Firefox and Safari won’t send them, so you’ll need a fallback. Where you can, feature detection beats browser detection anyway.

Here’s an uncomfortable truth: once a script runs on your page, it can call canvas, WebGL, and audio APIs, and there’s no header that switches those off. What you can control is which scripts run and how close they get to your page.

None of these is a silver bullet. Together, they cut down how much code gets the chance to fingerprint your users at all.

If your app draws on canvas (dashboards, editors, browser games), that output can be fingerprinted too. Try not to hand raw canvas data to third-party scripts.

Fonts count as well. Load fifteen unusual web fonts and you’ve given every script on the page an easy font fingerprint. A system font stack blends in better, and for interface text, most users won’t notice the difference.

Sometimes you’ll want to keep a fingerprint, for example to flag logins from a device you haven’t seen before. That’s fine, as long as you treat it with care:

Before you ship, open your site in Firefox with Enhanced Tracking Protection set to Strict, and in Brave with fingerprinting protection turned on. If something breaks, it was relying on a signal browsers are trying to get rid of.

Fix the feature. Don’t ask users to turn their protection down. Browsers are only going to get stricter from here.

What works better is a browser with fingerprinting protection built in, such as Brave, Firefox on strict settings, Safari, or Tor Browser. These either add noise to the signals or make everyone look the same. Extensions that block canvas and font reads can help too. So can simply updating your browser, since each release tends to remove a few more leaky details.

No single tool will stop fingerprinting completely. The good news is that it doesn’t have to. Fingerprinting works on probabilities, so making the signals noisier is often enough to break the match.

#10675. A tiny light trap could unlock million qubit quantum computers

After years of slow progress, researchers may finally be seeing a clear path forward in the quest to build powerful quantum computers. These machines are expected to dramatically shorten the time required for certain calculations, turning problems that would take classical computers thousands of years into tasks that could be completed in hours.

A team led by physicists at Stanford University has developed a new kind of optical cavity that can efficiently capture single photons, the basic particles of light, emitted by individual atoms. Those atoms serve as the core components of a quantum computer because they store qubits, which are the quantum equivalent of the zeros and ones used in traditional computing. For the first time, this approach allows information to be collected from all qubits at once.

Optical Cavities Enable Faster Qubit Readout

In research published in Nature, the team describes a system made up of 40 optical cavities, each holding a single atom qubit, along with a larger prototype that contains more than 500 cavities. The results point to a realistic route toward building quantum computing networks that could one day include as many as a million qubits.

"If we want to make a quantum computer, we need to be able to read information out of the quantum bits very quickly," said Jon Simon, the study's senior author and associate professor of physics and of applied physics in Stanford's School of Humanities and Sciences. "Until now, there hasn't been a practical way to do that at scale because atoms just don't emit light fast enough, and on top of that, they spew it out in all directions. An optical cavity can efficiently guide emitted light toward a particular direction, and now we've found a way to equip each atom in a quantum computer within its own individual cavity."

An optical cavity works by trapping light between two or more reflective surfaces, causing it to bounce back and forth. The effect can be compared to standing between mirrors in a fun house, where reflections seem to stretch endlessly into the distance. In scientific settings, these cavities are far smaller and use repeated passes of a laser beam to extract information from atoms.

Although optical cavities have been studied for decades, they have been difficult to use with atoms because atoms are extremely small and nearly transparent. Getting light to interact with them strongly enough has been a persistent challenge.

Rather than relying on many repeated reflections, the Stanford team introduced microlenses inside each cavity to tightly focus light onto a single atom. Even with fewer light bounces, this method proved more effective at pulling quantum information from the atom.

"We have developed a new type of cavity architecture; it's not just two mirrors anymore," said Adam Shaw, a Stanford Science Fellow and first author on the study. "We hope this will enable us to build dramatically faster, distributed quantum computers that can talk to each other with much faster data rates."

Beyond the Binary Limits of Classical Computing

Conventional computers process information using bits that represent either zero or one. Quantum computers operate using qubits, which are based on the quantum states of tiny particles. A qubit can represent zero, one, or both states at the same time, allowing quantum systems to handle certain calculations far more efficiently than classical machines.

"A classical computer has to churn through possibilities one by one, looking for the correct answer," said Simon. "But a quantum computer acts like noise-canceling headphones that compare combinations of answers, amplifying the right ones while muffling the wrong ones."

Scientists estimate that quantum computers will need millions of qubits to outperform today's most powerful supercomputers. According to Simon, reaching that level will likely require connecting many quantum computers into large networks. The parallel light-based interface demonstrated in this study provides an efficient foundation for scaling up to those sizes.

The researchers showed a working 40-cavity array in the current study, along with a proof-of-concept system containing more than 500 cavities. Their next goal is to expand to tens of thousands. Looking further ahead, the team envisions quantum data centers in which individual quantum computers are linked through cavity-based network interfaces to form full-scale quantum supercomputers.

Broader Scientific and Technological Impact

Significant engineering hurdles remain, but the researchers believe the potential benefits are substantial. Large-scale quantum computers could lead to breakthroughs in materials design and chemical synthesis, including applications related to drug discovery, as well as advances in code breaking.

The ability to efficiently collect light also has implications beyond computing. Cavity arrays could improve biosensing and microscopy, supporting progress in medical and biological research. Quantum networks may even contribute to astronomy by enabling optical telescopes with enhanced resolution, potentially allowing scientists to directly observe planets orbiting stars beyond our solar system.

"As we understand more about how to manipulate light at a single particle level, I think it will transform our ability to see the world," Shaw said.

​​Simon is also the Joan Reinhart Professor of Physics & Applied Physics. Shaw is also a Felix Bloch Fellow and an Urbanek-Chodorow Fellow.

Additional Stanford co-authors include David Schuster, the Joan Reinhart Professor of Applied Physics, and doctoral students Anna Soper, Danial Shadmany, and Da-Yeon Koh.

Other co-authors include researchers from Stony Brook University, the University of Chicago, Harvard University, and Montana State University.

This research received support from the National Science Foundation, Air Force Office of Scientific Research, Army Research Office, Hertz Foundation, and the U.S. Department of Defense.

Matt Jaffe of Montana State University and Simon act as consultants to and hold stock options in Atom Computing. Shadmany, Jaffe, Schuster, and Simon, as well as Aishwarya Kumar of Stony Brook, hold a patent on the resonator geometry demonstrated in this work.
